justification_text:
My point estimates reflect a modestly bullish but essentially range-bound view across all three horizons. At the one-day horizon, the estimate of 117.5 was anchored primarily to the prevailing price level at the time of the forecast, with only minimal drift expected given typical overnight and intraday volatility. At the one-week horizon, I nudged the estimate slightly higher to 118.0, reflecting a mild positive drift assumption consistent with the modest upward bias equity and risk assets have historically exhibited over short windows. The one-month estimate of 119.0 extends that same gentle drift further, implying no strong directional catalyst but acknowledging that the path of least resistance, absent new information, tends to follow the recent trend.

The confidence interval widths expand meaningfully as the horizon lengthens, which reflects the standard statistical reality that uncertainty compounds over time. At one day, a plus-or-minus three-point range captures the typical daily volatility one might expect under normal market conditions. By one week, that range widens to plus-or-minus six points, incorporating the possibility of a few consecutive volatile sessions or a single macro surprise. At one month, the interval stretches to plus-or-minus thirteen points, acknowledging that a full month introduces earnings releases, central bank decisions, geopolitical developments, and shifting sentiment cycles — all of which can meaningfully reprice assets.

There are several specific risks that could push outcomes well outside my stated intervals. On the downside, a surprise tightening in financial conditions — such as an unexpected central bank hawkish pivot, a credit event, or a sharp deterioration in economic data — could push prices below the lower bounds. Geopolitical escalation or a sudden liquidity shock could amplify that downside move sharply. On the upside, a stronger-than-expected earnings season, a dovish policy shift, or a significant improvement in macro sentiment could push prices above the upper bounds, particularly at the one-month horizon where there is more time for such catalysts to materialize and compound.

It is also worth acknowledging that my intervals, while calibrated to represent 90% coverage, are inherently model-dependent and carry their own uncertainty. Real-world return distributions have fatter tails than normal distributions imply, meaning truly extreme events — flash crashes, sudden geopolitical shocks, or systemic financial stress — occur more frequently than a simple symmetric interval would suggest. Readers should treat the outer bounds not as hard limits but as reasonable guides around the central scenario, understanding that tail outcomes beyond those bounds, while unlikely, are never negligible.
